sections.heading: Coming to you with a full heart
sections.text: My God, you are more beautiful, greater, and more worthy than anything else I could ever love. My heart is drawn to you in wonder, worship, and love. I feel like a small cup filled to the brim, and I want to pour out everything in me before you in praise.
theological_themes: God is supremely worthy of love and worship.
Human praise is a response to God's own beauty, greatness, and goodness.
Gratitude overflows when the heart sees God clearly.

scripture_references.connection: David speaks of longing for God himself and responding with praise because God's steadfast love is better than life. This supports the prayer's movement from admiration of God to overflowing worship.
This verse grounds the claim that God's greatness is beyond full human expression, while still calling his people to praise him.

sections.heading: Finding joy in knowing you
sections.text: When I turn my mind toward you and speak with you, joy opens up in places I did not know were closed. Thoughts of you refresh me. Your presence fills ordinary moments with more gladness than anything else can give.
theological_themes: Communion with God brings deep joy and renewal.
Prayer and meditation on God are not merely duties but sources of delight.
God himself is the believer's highest happiness.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm presents fullness of joy as being found in God's presence. That directly supports the prayer's claim that knowing and speaking with God refreshes the heart.
Paul connects rejoicing in the Lord with prayerful communion and God's guarding peace. This illuminates the prayer's sense that turning toward God changes the inner life.

sections.heading: Thanking you for soul and body
sections.text: Thank you for the life you have given me. Thank you for making me a living soul, and for not leaving me as I am, but working in me, cleansing me, and teaching me to belong to you—even when my heart still feels like hard ground. Thank you for my body: for strength, movement, breath, senses, and the simple ability to taste, see, hear, touch, work, and respond to the world you made. Every ordinary capacity I have is a gift from you.
theological_themes: God is Creator and giver of both soul and body.
Sanctification is God's gracious work in a person who still feels inward barrenness.
Ordinary physical abilities are gifts to be received with gratitude.

scripture_references.connection: This passage portrays human life as personally given by God, grounding thanks for both bodily existence and living soul.
Paul prays for God to sanctify his people completely and anchors that hope in God's faithfulness. This fits the prayer's gratitude that God adorns and sanctifies the soul despite remaining weakness.
Paul teaches that God gives life, breath, and everything to all people. This supports thanksgiving for ordinary physical life and capacities as dependent gifts from God.

sections.heading: Receiving your daily kindness
sections.text: Thank you for your generous care in the details of my life: food on the table, a cup that is more than enough, appetite, taste, sweetness, rest, and daily help. I do not want to treat these things as automatic or deserved. They come from your open hand.
theological_themes: God provides daily needs through his providential generosity.
Material blessings are to be received with humility and thanksgiving.
Creaturely enjoyment can be an act of worship when received from God.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm praises God for providing food, wine, oil, and bread that sustain and gladden human life. It supports gratitude for ordinary provision and enjoyment.
Paul teaches that God's created gifts are good when received with thanksgiving. This directly bears on thanking God for food, taste, and daily comforts.

sections.heading: Thanking you for people and usefulness
sections.text: Thank you for the joy of family and friends, for the comfort of shared life, and for the chance to love people who are near me. Thank you for giving me ways to serve others. Thank you for a heart that can feel another person's sorrow and need, a mind that can care about my neighbors, and opportunities to bring some happiness and help into the lives around me.
theological_themes: Love for neighbor includes compassion, practical service, and shared joy.
Human abilities and opportunities are entrusted by God for the good of others.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes Christian life as brotherly affection, honor, generosity, and hospitality. This supports the prayer's thanksgiving for relationships and opportunities to serve.
This passage urges believers to keep doing good, especially as opportunities arise. It fits the prayer's gratitude for chances to spread help and happiness around.
Paul says God comforts his people so they can comfort others. This supports the prayer's gratitude for a heart that can enter into others' sorrows and needs.

sections.heading: Hoping for the day I see you clearly
sections.text: Thank you for loved ones who are already with you in the joy of heaven. Thank you that my own hope is not limited to this life, but is set on the day when I will see you clearly and be with you forever. I love you more than I know how to say, because of who you are and because of how generous you are to all you have made. Please grow my love for you through every season of this life, and keep growing it into eternity.
theological_themes: Christian hope includes life with God beyond death.
Believers long to see God clearly and fully.
Love for God is already real but still needs to grow by God's grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts present partial knowledge with the future clarity of seeing fully. This grounds the prayer's longing to see God clearly.
Paul describes being away from the body as being at home with the Lord for the believer. This supports the hope concerning loved ones who have died in Christ and the believer's own future hope.
Paul prays that love would abound more and more until the day of Christ. This supports asking God to increase love through time and into final fulfillment.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original gives thanks for 'a full table and overflowing cup,' which may reflect material abundance not shared by every Christian. The adaptation keeps the concrete image but frames it as humble reception of God's provision rather than a universal assumption of wealth.

The line about 'loved ones in the joys of heaven' assumes those loved ones died in faith. The adaptation preserves the hope but states it in explicitly Christian terms by referring to loved ones being with God, without implying universalism.

The original's phrase that the soul is 'fixed in barren soil' could sound like creation itself is bad or that the body is spiritually inferior. The adaptation interprets it as the believer's awareness of remaining inward hardness and need for sanctification, not as contempt for embodied life.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated the opening image of the 'little vessel' as a heart filled to overflowing with gratitude, rather than as a claim of spiritual fullness or self-sufficiency.
I rendered 'converse with thee' as turning the mind toward God and speaking with him, preserving both meditation and prayer without using archaic devotional language.

I kept the original's broad thanksgiving for bodily senses and abilities in concrete form, because the prayer's theology includes gratitude for embodied creaturely life, not only for inward spiritual blessings.
I interpreted 'ability to serve others' and 'opportunities of spreading happiness around' as neighbor-love and practical service, avoiding a merely sentimental reading of making people happy.
